Fix the setting of PF_SUPERPRIV by __capable() as it could corrupt the flags
the target process if that is not the current process and it is trying to
change its own flags in a different way at the same time.
__capable() is using neither atomic ops nor locking to protect t->flags.  This
patch removes __capable() and introduces has_capability() that doesn't set
PF_SUPERPRIV on the process being queried.
This patch further splits security_ptrace() in two:
(1) security_ptrace_may_access().  This passes judgement on whether one
process may access another only (PTRACE_MODE_ATTACH for ptrace() and
PTRACE_MODE_READ for /proc)
column2: and takes a pointer to the child process.

column1: current is the parent.
(2) security_ptrace_traceme().  This passes judgement on PTRACE_TRACEME only
and takes only a pointer to the parent process.  current is the child.
In Smack and commoncap
column2: this uses has_capability() to determine whether

column1: the parent will be permitted to use PTRACE_ATTACH if normal checks fail.
This does not set PF_SUPERPRIV.
Two of the instances of __capable() actually only act on current
been changed to calls to capable().
Of the places that were using __capable():
(1) The OOM killer calls __capable() thrice when weighing the killability of a
process.  All of these now use has_capability().
(2) cap_ptrace() and smack_ptrace() were using __capable() to check to see
whether the parent was allowed to trace any process.  As mentioned above
these have been split.  For PTRACE_ATTACH and /proc
used
(3) cap_safe_nice() only ever saw current
(4) smack_setprocattr() rejected accesses to tasks other than current just
after calling __capable()
column2: so the order of these two tests have been

column1: switched and capable() is used instead.
(5) In smack_file_send_sigiotask()
column2: we need to allow privileged processes to

column1: receive SIGIO on files they're manipulating.
(6) In smack_task_wait()
column2: we let a process wait for a privileged process

column1: whether or not the process doing the waiting is privileged.
I've tested this with the LTP SELinux and syscalls testscripts.
